sources.headline: Deal or escalation? Beaten in US midterms, Trump faces stark choice on Iran
sources.text: DUBAI - US President Donald Trump went to war seeking regime change in Iran. Instead, it was his own grip on Washington that gave way, as voters weary of the war and hit by soaring fuel prices handed Democrats control of Congress.That leaves a weakened president facing a choice between a negotiated exit and a riskier escalation.In Tehran and among its allies, the result was swiftly cast as a verdict on the conflict. Across the Gulf, officials were left wondering which way Trump would turn.“Iran succeeded in regime change in America,” was the first reaction of one source close to a US Gulf ally.Officials in the Gulf states were stunned into silence by the scale of the Democratic sweep in the Nov 3 US midterm elections, the source said.The war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Feb 28 spread across the region as Tehran fired missiles and drones at Gulf targets and shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, disrupting global energy supplies. The US-Israeli campaign badly damaged Iran’s military capabilities but failed to deliver a decisive outcome, leaving the issue of Iran’s nuclear programme unresolved.A weakened Trump, facing a Democratic Congress able to constrain his military options, has greater incentive to seek a deal, said two sources close to Gulf government circles. A full-scale assault on Iran now looks less likely, they said. Further limited strikes on nuclear facilities may offer the US a way to claim its objectives had been met and draw a line under the conflict, as China steps up efforts to broker a settlement.Yet, an agreement that allows Iran to claim clear victory and leaves Trump looking defeated can provoke recklessness as readily as restraint, Gulf analysts said.The rebuke from the US electorate came a week after Israeli voters delivered their own blow to the war’s other architect, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. His right-wing bloc won 53 of the Knesset’s 120 seats in the Oct 27 election, eight short of a majority, leaving him fighting to retain power.Two beleaguered leaders, each with his political future increasingly tied to the war’s outcome, may come to see escalation not as a risk but as a way out of their political predicament. Such a calculation may be irrational, but no less dangerous.Risk of miscalculation“The US election results make a settlement more urgent for Trump, but no easier for Iran,” said Ebtesam al-Ketbi, president of the Emirates Policy Centre in Abu Dhabi.Much hinges, she said, on how Tehran reads the moment. “If Tehran recognises that Trump needs a deal, but not just any deal, a genuine opportunity could emerge to end the war. But if it interprets the results as evidence that American resolve has weakened, it could instead encourage him to launch a new military escalation.”Gulf states want the election to open a path to ending the war, but not at any cost, al-Ketbi said. Any settlement that disregards freedom of navigation through Hormuz, allows Iran to impose tolls or political conditions on shipping, or leaves Gulf states exposed to military threats would be a temporary arrangement that lays the groundwork for another crisis.In Tehran, leaders savoured Trump’s humiliation but did not lower their guard, with Iran’s chief negotiator hailing a “NO TO WAR” result.Two senior Iranian sources said Tehran remained on high alert, fearing Trump could try to make up for his defeat with a military strike. Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei warned against “even the slightest inclination towards submission”, a signal that Iran has no intention of softening its demands over the Strait of Hormuz.Emirati political analyst Abdulkhaleq Abdulla argued that the greater danger now stems from Iran, rather than the US or Israel. Iran’s leaders, he said, have long been “arrogant”, overestimating their own strength and underestimating American and Israeli military power. That mindset persists, he said, providing ample reason not to rule out another bout of fighting.“The Iranians have more today to brag about. If anyone drags us into another war, it won’t be Netanyahu, it won’t be Trump, but the guys in Tehran. They might grossly miscalculate that Trump is weak and Netanyahu is finished, and up the ante.”Wariness over expected probesAbdulaziz Sager, chairman of the Saudi-based Gulf Research Centre, warned that defeat could make Trump more willing to strike, not less. With the midterms behind him and no third term ahead, the electoral considerations that once encouraged restraint have diminished. That leaves a president with less to lose and a legacy to secure.Trump, he said, may see confrontation with Iran as a chance to “finish the job” before leaving office. “If Iran continues to resist... and emerges claiming victory, Trump may feel compelled to act to prevent that outcome and claim a clear success for his presidency.”Lebanese political commentator Sarkis Naoum said Trump’s defeat had weakened his hand with Iran, leaving him with diminished leverage at the negotiating table and fewer options to secure a deal.An official from Iran-backed Hezbollah said the threat of war had not necessarily receded and that “reckless moves” remained a possibility.“At this moment, the chances of escalation and de-escalation may be equal,” he said.Once seated in Congress in January, Democrats are expected to use their power to investigate Trump’s administration, family and allies and demand concessions on major legislation.For US allies in the Gulf, the political shift in Washington carries risks that extend well beyond the war itself. A source close to government thinking said Gulf states were wary of probes that they expected to be launched into business by their own entities with the Trump family. REUTERS

sources.headline: As Trump’s Midterm Deadline Looms, Gulf Countries Brace for Possible Renewal of Iran War
sources.text: The energy-rich Gulf Arab countries are engaged in a flurry of mediation efforts to avert war between the U.S. and Iran, as many fear that the fighting will be worse this time around.

sources.headline: Will the US resume its attacks on Iran?
sources.text:
Inside StoryTehran says it’s ready with a maximum deterrence plan.“Our response will be without geographical restrictions.”That’s the warning from Iran as fears grow that the United States could renew all-out war after US President Donald Trump warned his country could attack Iran once US midterm elections were over.Trump’s Republican Party suffered a severe blow in the congressional elections, losing its majority in both the House and the Senate. And Trump has conceded that the US-Israel war with Iran was partly to blame.With the region on edge again, mediators have been trying to bring Tehran and Washington closer to a peace deal. sources.headline: Can US midterm election really change Trump's Iran policy?
sources.text:
Tuesday's election is shaping up to be one of the most consequential midterm votes in modern US history, with Washington's relationship with Israel and its war on Iran at the center of the political standoff.
Many Democrats, including the party's rising stars such as Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, are outspoken critics of the Iran war. El-Sayed called the conflict "illegal" and "stupid."
US President Donald Trump sought to downplay the effects of the war during the campaign. Last week, he claimed only "one or two targets" remained in Iran and that those could be settled in 10 minutes. However, he immediately added that messages were still being exchanged, Tehran still shows strong interest in a deal, and the US has plenty of time to deal with the crisis.
At the same time, there are reports of the US and Israel preparing to launch a new round of strikes on Iran just after the midterm election . Pro-war Republicans such as Senator Ted Cruz are putting pressure on the White House to deal with "the threat" posed by Iran.
"I have urged arming the Iranian protesters to overthrow the regime," Cruz said in an online post after spending a day with Trump.
Behind the scenes, analysts warn that the Washington political elite may not be as divided on Iran as it appears. Moreover, even a resounding Democrat victory might not give them enough leverage on the Trump administration regarding the Iran war.
Democrats and Republicans broadly 'in consensus' on Iran
Talking to DW, former National Security Advisor John Bolton said the Democrats are likely to secure a majority in the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate, handing them control of the Iran war funding.
The US Congress "can allocate defense budgets or impose restrictions on the use of financial resources," Bolton said.
Iran conflict: Could a new phase of the war be imminent?To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Nevertheless, Bolton pointed out that the US president can veto congressional legislation, which would then require a two-thirds majority in both assemblies to overcome.
"Even if Democrats hold a majority in both houses, their influence will be limited to the legislative and political tools of Congress," he said.
US diplomat and Iran expert Alan Eyre, a fellow at the Middle East Institute, described a kind of "bipartisan consensus" that Republicans and Democrats have on Iran.
"Both major US parties share significant common ground in their opposition to the political structure of the Islamic Republic and in their support for policies aimed at exerting pressure on Tehran to change its behavior," he said.What does Tehran think?
While warning of a "crushing response" to any new strikes on underground sites, Tehran has confirmed ongoing indirect communication via Doha and Muscat, keeping its diplomatic option open.
Shahin Modarres, an international security analyst leading the Iran team at ITSS Verona, told DW that Tehran's actions are based on a miscalculation. The regime, he argued, assumes that a Democratic Congress can easily restrain the White House.
Tehran's strategy in dragging out peace talks, pressuring the Strait of Hormuz, and letting fuel prices weigh on US voters, aims to deny Trump a win before November. However, Modarres noted this strategy may backfire after the election, when the Trump administration will no longer have any reason to delay its moves.
This approach also ignores the fact that both US parties largely agree on not letting Iranian develop nuclear weapons, he said.How serious are Iran's new threats of retaliation?To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Will Trump launch new strikes and declare victory?
Trump's ally-turned-critic John Bolton believes the president will only decide on his next steps on Iran after the election, once the political pressure grows less acute.
"I cannot predict what the US President will do; even Trump himself does not know his final decision right now," he told DW.
Bolton cites as an example a possible US attack on "Kuh-e Kolang," the new nuclear site he claims the Iranian government is constructing near Natanz.
"In this scenario, Trump could damage these facilities, declare victory, and pull back."
Bolton: 'Regime change' only guarantee against Iran getting nukes
Trump has consistently emphasized that the US goal is to deny Iran the capability of acquiring nuclear weapons. Throughout the conflict, the US president has also repeatedly claimed his administration had succeeded in this regard.
Bolton, in contrast, believes that the Islamic Republic will continue to pursue nuclear weapons capability for as long as it remains in power.
The former Trump advisor views "regime change" as the only sustainable solution to keep Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons.US military buildup: What message is it sending Iran?To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
US failing to communicate with ordinary Iranians
Eyre emphasized the difficulty of using external tools to bring about sustainable change. In his view, even if there is a consensus in Washington opposing the Islamic Republic and demanding a change in its behavior, this US consensus alone cannot overcome the structural obstacles to political change inside Iran. He reiterated that any fundamental transformation must emerge from within Iranian society itself.
The veteran diplomat also pointed to the failure of American diplomacy to "convey a clear, coherent, and authentic message to Iranian society."
He noted that official US government messaging is only incompletely reflected in the media outlets that the vast majority of Iranian citizens rely on for news.
"Furthermore, targeted and principled engagement with the core of Iranian society has generally not been a priority for successive US administrations," he said. "Iranian citizens see that the US takes certain positions at the rhetorical level, but behaves differently in practice."
According to Eyre, this gap between words and deeds in Washington is a structural phenomenon that is not limited to a single administration or a single election cycle.Iran's regime: inside the system protecting its rulers To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

sources.headline: US midterms 2026: Could a Trump defeat in Congress alter the Iran war?
sources.text: File photo: How US midterms could shape Trump’s next move in the Iran warThe outcome of the US midterm elections could reshape the political constraints on US president Donald Trump’s war with Iran, even if it does not directly determine the course of the military campaign.A Democratic takeover of the House of Representatives would give the opposition greater power to investigate the administration’s handling of the conflict, question its objectives and press for limits on further military action. But Trump would remain commander-in-chief, with the authority to direct US military operations.Congress does have powers over war and military spending, but using them to force a president to change course is difficult. Trump could veto legislation seeking to restrict military operations, and overriding that veto would require a two-thirds majority in both chambers, a threshold Democrats are unlikely to reach even if they make significant gains. Lawmakers may also be reluctant to cut funding for American troops already deployed in the region.The political pressure could nevertheless influence Trump's calculations. The Iran war has become a domestic issue as its economic consequences, particularly rising energy prices and the cost of living, weigh on voters. A recent survey cited by the Washington Examiner found that more than 70% of Americans wanted Congress to prioritise lowering living costs and ending the war in 2027. Discontent has also emerged within Trump's MAGA base, where opposition to overseas military involvement has challenged his earlier “America First” promises.There are also questions over whether the administration could resume or expand military action after the elections. NPR reported that US and Israeli preparations for a possible renewed round of attacks have fuelled expectations of escalation after the midterms. The US has two aircraft carriers in the Arabian Sea, with a third on the way, while US allies in the region have stepped up military exercises. These developments do not confirm that an attack is imminent, but point to the possibility of a wider campaign.Trump could therefore face three broad paths after the vote: pull back and seek a negotiated settlement, maintain the current pressure through the blockade and targeted strikes, or escalate the campaign against Iran and its regional allies. The election result may alter the political costs of each option, but the most consequential decisions will remain with the White House.
